source_text: τοῦτο μοι ἀποβήσεται εἰς σωτηρίαν, διὰ τῆς ὑμῶν δεήσεως καὶ ἐπιχορηγίας τοῦ πνεύματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ»· 2.20 ἄθρει δὴ οὖν, ὡς καὶ μόνον τὸ φάναι αὐτὸ «πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ», καὶ ἡ προσθήκη δὲ τοῦ «μοῦ» καὶ «σοῦ», καὶ τοῦτο τηλαυγῶς ἐσήμανεν, ὅτι καὶ ἄκτιστόν ἐστι καὶ θεός, τοὔνομα ἔχον οὐκ ἐπακτόν, ἀλλ' ἀπὸ τοῦ εἶναι ἐκεῖνο φυσικῶς τοῦτο ὅπερ καὶ προσηγορεύεται. 2.21 καὶ τὸ γεγράφθαι δὲ αὐτὸ «πνεῦμα τοῦ υἱοῦ», ὁμοίως τὴν πρὸς αὐτὸν κοινωνίαν τῆς φύσεως ἐδήλωσεν, καὶ ὥστε μὴ κτίσμα αὐτοῦ νομισθῆναι. πῶς γὰρ ἂν τῷ ἰδίῳ πατρί, ὡς οὐκ ἔχοντι πρὸ τούτου ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ, ἔκτισεν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦθ' ὅπερ ἔστι τε καὶ γέγραπται πνεῦμα θεοῦ; ὅπερ οὐ βλάσφημόν ἐστι μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἠλίθιον. νοηθείη ἂν «πνεῦμα Χριστοῦ», τουτέστιν δύναμις Χριστοῦ, ὃν τρόπον εἴρηται «Χριστὸν θεοῦ δύναμιν καὶ θεοῦ σοφίαν.» 44 ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἑνὸς πατρὸς φύσει καὶ οὐ δημιουργικῇ ἐνεργείᾳ προῆλθον αἱ μακάριαι ὑποστάσεις αὖται, εἰς τὸν αὐτὸν ἕνα ἀνάγονται. 2.22 ἵνα γὰρ μή τις ὑποπτεύσῃ ἀρχὴν αὐτοῦ εἶναι ἢ πέρας, ἀλλ' ἀπὸ τῆς κατὰ τὴν φύσιν αὐτοῦ προόδου πιστεύσῃ ἀληθῶς αὐτὸ πνεῦμα εἶναι τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀναπνευσθὲν ἀνάρχως, καὶ οὐ γενόμενον, ὡς ἓν τῶν ἄλλων λειτουργικῶν πνευμάτων, διδάσκων ὁ κύριος ἐν τῷ κατὰ Ἰωάννην εὐαγγελίῳ λέγει· «τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας, ὃ παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ἐκπορεύεται». οὐκ εἶπεν δὲ «κτίζεται». πᾶσα μὲν γὰρ γέννησις καὶ ἐκπόρευσις διὰ τῶν ἴσων καὶ ὁμοίων ἐπιτελεῖται· μάλιστα δὲ διαφερόντως ἡ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑνὸς πατρὸς καθ' ἕνωσιν τῆς ἑαυτοῦ θεότητός ἐστι γέννησις καὶ ἐκπόρευσις. 2.23 ἀλλ' ἐπὶ μὲν τῶν κτισμάτων ἡγεῖται τῷ χρόνῳ ὁ πρωτότυπος· ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ οὐχ οὕτως, ἀλλὰ συνυφεστώτως καὶ συμπροεληλυθότως. 2.24 συνᾴδων δὲ τῷ κυρίῳ καὶ Ἰωάννης ἐκήρυξεν τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος τὸ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα ἴσον καὶ ἀπαράλλακτον καὶ ὡς μερικὴ αὐτοῦ χάρις ὅλον, ὡς ἂν εἴποι τις, τὸν ἀπερίγραφον θεὸν πατέρα περιλαμβάνον, καὶ ὡς μερικὴ χάρις παρὰ πιστοῖς εὑρισκόμενον δείκνυσιν, εἰπών· «ἐν τούτῳ γὰρ γινώσκομεν, ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ μένομεν, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν ἡμῖν ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος αὐτοῦ, οὗ ἔδωκεν ἡμῖν». ὃν τρόπον ὁ υἱὸς εἶπεν· «ὁ ἑορακὼς ἐμὲ τὸν πατέρα·» καί· «ἐγὼ παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ἐξῆλθον.» 2.25 οὐδὲν γὰρ ὅλως κατ' οὐσίαν ἢ κατὰ χρόνον ἢ δόξαν ὕφεσιν ἔχον δύναται τὴν ὅλην ἐκφαίνειν ἀλήθειαν ἢ ὁμοειδὲς τυγχάνειν καὶ ἴσην ἔχειν ἐπίγνωσιν· οὔτε δέ τις τύχοι ἂν μετοχῆς θεότητος ἀληθοῦς διὰ κτίσματος· 2.26 δίδοται δὲ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, οὐ κατατομῆς μερισμοῖς, ἀλλὰ τῷ λόγῳ τῆς μετουσίας, καὶ τοῦ μὴ νοεῖσθαι ἑτεροφυῶς ἢ ἑτερογνωμόνως τοῦ πατρὸς οἰκεῖν ἐν ἡμῖν. 2.27 ἔδειξεν δὲ ἅμα «ὁ τῆς βροντῆς υἱὸς», ὡς ἔνθα ἐστὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, πάρεστιν ὁ θεὸς πατήρ, οὗ πνεῦμά ἐστιν· ὅπερ καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ θεὸς προανεφώνησεν, εἰπών· «ἐνοικήσω ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ ἐμπεριπατήσω· καὶ ἔσομαι αὐτῶν θεός, καὶ αὐτοὶ ἔσονταί μου λαός.» 2.28 ὡς πάλιν τὸ ἀντικείμενον δηλοῖ, ὅτι εἴ τις τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ ὡς θεὸν ἀληθινὸν οὐκ ἔχει, οὐδὲ τὸν πατέρα ἔχει· παρ' οἷς δὲ μὴ οὗτός ἐστιν, οὐδὲν ἀληθὲς οὐδ' ἀσφαλὲς οὐδὲ βέβαιον. 2.29 ὡς τὸ ἔμπαλιν ὁστισοῦν λέγων περὶ αὐτοῦ, κἂν αἱρετικὸς ὢν τύχοι, ἐὰν ἐρωτηθῇ, περὶ ποίου διαλέγεται πνεύματος, λέγει· «τοῦ ἁγίου»· καὶ εἰ αὖθις πάλιν πεῦσις αὐτῷ προσενεχθείη, «ποίου ἁγίου», ἀνάγκη αὐτὸν εἰπεῖν εἰς φανερωτάτην δήλωσιν· «τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ θεοῦ», ὡς τῶν ἄλλων μὴ οὐσιωδῶς ὄντων αὐτοῦ. 2.30 μοχθηροὶ δὲ ἑαυτοῖς τε καὶ τοῖς ἀκούουσιν γινόμενοι αἱρετικοί, βιαίοις ἐπιχειρήσεσιν συκοφαντοῦσι τοὺς ἡμῶν καὶ αὐτῶν ἀμείνους καὶ μέγιστον διαφέροντας καὶ περὶ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος χρήσαντας ἁγίους· οἷς οὐκ ἐναντία νομοθετητέον. 2.31 φασὶν γὰρ κατὰ λέξιν οὕτως· «ὅταν οὖν λέγῃ ὁ θεός· «ὁ παῖς μου Ἡσαῖας·» καὶ, «υἱὸς πρωτότοκός μου Ἰσραήλ», ἡ «μοῦ» συλλαβὴ ἔχειν τι κοινὸν τὴν ἀνθρωπείαν φύσιν πρὸς τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ δείκνυσιν; ὥσπερ οὖν, φησίν, τοῦτο εἶπεν ὡς τοῦ εἶναι αὐτοῖς αἴτιος. οὕτως καὶ τὴν ψύχωσιν αὐτῶν «πνεῦμά μου» προσεῖπεν.» 2.32 εἴ τις δὲ αὐτοῖς τῆς ἀληθείας καὶ ἀκριβείας λόγος ὑπῆν, οὐκ ἂν τηλικαῦτα ἔπταιον. πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ αὐτῷ τῷ φάναι «Ἡσαῖαν» καὶ «Ἰσραὴλ» ἀνθρώπους ἐδήλωσεν· προσέθηκεν δὲ κατ' ἐξαίρετον αὐτοῖς τὸ «μοῦ» ὡς αὐτῷ ταῖς πράξεσιν προσήκουσιν. 2.33 τὸν Ἡσαῖαν δὲ «παῖδα» ἐκάλεσεν, τουτέστιν οἰκέτην, τὸν δὲ Ἰσραὴλ «πρωτότοκον», ὡς πρῶτον ἀρξάμενον λατρεύειν αὐτῷ, καὶ ὄντα τῇ περὶ αὐτὸν διαθέσει καὶ φροντίδι τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν τάξει υἱοῦ. 2.34 ὥστε τὸ «μοῦ» ἐπὶ τοῦ

For how would the Son have created for his own Father, as not having [it] from himself before this, this very thing which both is and has been written 'spirit of God'? Which is not blasphemous only, but also foolish. 'Spirit of Christ' might be understood, that is, power of Christ, in the way it has been said: 'Christ power of God and wisdom of God'. For since by nature of one Father, and not by creative activity, these blessed hypostases went forth, they are led back to the same one. 2.22 For so that no one suspect there to be a beginning of it or an end, but from the procession according to its nature may believe it truly to be spirit of God, breathed out without beginning, and not having come to be, as one of the other ministering spirits, the Lord, teaching in the gospel according to John, says: 'the spirit of the truth, which proceeds from the Father'. But he did not say 'is created'. For every begetting and procession is accomplished through equal and like things; but most of all, distinctively, is the begetting and procession from the one Father according to the union of his own Godhead. 2.23 But in the case of the creatures the original leads in time; but in the case of God not so, but co-subsistingly and having come forth together. 2.24 And singing in agreement with the Lord John too proclaimed the equal and unvarying of the Holy Spirit toward the Father, and shows [it] as a partial grace of his, embracing, as one might say, the whole uncircumscribed God the Father, and as a partial grace being found among believers, saying: 'for in this we know that we remain in him, and he in us, from his spirit, which he gave us'. pass_b_english: … this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:19).

Observe, then, how merely calling him “Spirit of God”, and adding “my” and “your”, has also signified this plainly: that he is uncreated and God, and that he holds the name not as something brought in from outside, but because by nature he is the very thing he is called.

And that he is written “Spirit of the Son” likewise showed his fellowship of nature with the Son, so that he should not be thought the Son’s creature. For how could the Son have created for his own Father, as though the Father did not have it from himself before, that which both is and is written “Spirit of God”? That is not only blasphemous but foolish as well. “Spirit of Christ” may be understood as “power of Christ”, in the way it is said: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). For since these blessed hypostases came forth from the nature of one Father, and not by a creative act, they are traced back to the same One.

For so that no one may suspect that he has a beginning or an end, but may truly believe, from the procession that belongs to his nature, that he is the Spirit of God, breathed forth without beginning and not made like one of the other ministering spirits, the Lord teaches in the Gospel according to John and says: “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26). He did not say “is created”. For every begetting and every procession is brought about through what is equal and alike; and most of all, beyond every other, is the begetting and procession from the one Father, in the unity of his own Godhead. But among creatures the original goes before in time; with God it is not so: they subsist together and have come forth together.

In harmony with the Lord, John too proclaimed that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and does not differ from him. He shows that the Spirit, a partial grace of the Father, embraces, so to speak, the whole of God the Father, who cannot be circumscribed, and is found among the faithful as a partial grace, when he says: “For by this we know that we abide in him and he in us, by his Spirit, whom he has given us” (1 John 4:13). In the same way the Son said: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9); and: “I came forth from the Father” (John 16:28).

For nothing at all that falls short in essence, or in time, or in glory, can display the whole truth, or be of the same kind and have equal knowledge; nor could anyone gain a share in true Godhead through a creature. The Holy Spirit is given, not by cutting him into portions, but on the principle of participation, and so that he may not be thought to dwell in us as one different from the Father in nature or in will.

At the same time “the son of thunder” (Mark 3:17) showed that where the Holy Spirit is, God the Father is present, whose Spirit he is. God himself proclaimed this beforehand when he said: “I will dwell in them and walk among them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (2 Corinthians 6:16). So again the opposite makes plain that whoever does not have the Spirit of God as true God does not have the Father either; and where he is not, there is nothing true, nothing safe, nothing firm.

So, conversely, anyone at all who speaks of him, even if he happens to be a heretic, if asked what spirit he is talking about, says, “The Holy Spirit”; and if the question is put to him again, “Which Holy Spirit?”, he must say, to make it as plain as possible, “The Spirit of God”, since the other spirits are not his in essence.

But the heretics, a trouble to themselves and to their hearers, slander with violent arguments the saints who are better than both us and them, who far surpass us, and who uttered oracles about the Holy Spirit; and no one may lay down rules against them. For they say, word for word: “When God says, ‘My servant Isaiah’ (Isaiah 20:3), and ‘Israel my firstborn son’ (Exodus 4:22), does the syllable ‘my’ show that human nature has something in common with the nature of God? Just as he said this, then,” he says, “as the cause of their being, so too he called the life of their souls ‘my spirit’.”

If they had any regard for truth and precision, they would not have stumbled so badly. For first, by the very names “Isaiah” and “Israel” he showed that they were men; and he added the “my” to them as a special honour, as men who belonged to him by their deeds. He called Isaiah “servant”, that is, a member of his household, and Israel “firstborn”, as the first to begin to worship him, and as standing in the rank of a son through God’s favour and care toward him. choices.issue: Old draft dropped 2.25-2.26 and garbled the rest
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English broke off in 2.24 ('For nothing at all according to essence...') and resumed mid-2.26 ('not by divisions of cutting'), dropping 2.25 (nothing that falls short in essence, time or glory can display the whole truth or share equal knowledge; no one gains a share in Godhead through a creature) and the subject of 2.26 ('the Holy Spirit is given'). It read the added 'my' (μοῦ) in 2.20 as 'of', ἠλίθιον (foolish) as 'a lie', made 2.21's quotation 'the power of Christ', rendered λειτουργικῶν (ministering) as 'functional', ἀναπνευσθὲν ἀνάρχως as 'breathed uncaused', συνυφεστώτως (subsisting together) as 'co-essential', ὕφεσις unrendered, and ran 2.26-2.34 into one block. References added: Philippians 1:19, 1 Corinthians 1:24, 2 Corinthians 6:16, Isaiah 20:3, Exodus 4:22, Mark 3:17. Kept: John 15:26, 1 John 4:13, John 14:9, John 16:28.

choices.english: … this will turn out for my salvation
choices.why: The section opens mid-quotation; the previous section ends “For I know that …”. Only this section's words are translated.
The pronouns of 'my spirit' and 'your holy spirit' in the texts just quoted; the old draft read μοῦ as 'of'.

choices.term: νοηθείη ἂν «πνεῦμα Χριστοῦ», τουτέστιν δύναμις Χριστοῦ
choices.english: “Spirit of Christ” may be understood as “power of Christ”
choices.why: The genitive marks belonging by nature, as 'power of God' does of Christ in 1 Corinthians 1:24, not a thing made.
ἄναρχος here is 'without beginning' in time, matching 'beginning or end' earlier in the sentence.

choices.term: μάλιστα δὲ διαφερόντως … καθ' ἕνωσιν τῆς ἑαυτοῦ θεότητος
choices.english: and most of all, beyond every other, … in the unity of his own Godhead
choices.why: Two intensifiers kept; κατά with ἕνωσις gives the ground of the equality.

choices.english: they subsist together and have come forth together
choices.why: Adverbs turned into a clause; contrasted with creatures, where the original precedes in time.

choices.term: ὡς μερικὴ αὐτοῦ χάρις ὅλον … τὸν ἀπερίγραφον θεὸν πατέρα περιλαμβάνον
choices.english: the Spirit, a partial grace of the Father, embraces, so to speak, the whole of God the Father, who cannot be circumscribed
choices.why: ὅλον agrees with πατέρα: given in part to believers, the Spirit still contains the whole Father (compare 2.27). Didymus' hedge 'so to speak' kept.

choices.english: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father”
choices.why: Didymus cites the verse in shortened form without the second verb; English needs the verb, so it is supplied from the verse he cites, without a bracket.
λόγος here is the rationale or principle, contrasted with 'cutting into portions'.

choices.term: περὶ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος χρήσαντας ἁγίους
choices.english: the saints … who uttered oracles about the Holy Spirit
choices.why: χράω is to give an oracle; Didymus means the inspired writers whose texts he has just quoted.

choices.english: and no one may lay down rules against them
choices.why: Verbal adjective of obligation; the inspired saints are not to be overruled by contrary rules.
ψύχωσις is the giving of soul-life; the heretics take 'my spirit' to mean the human soul God gives, not the Holy Spirit.
Didymus glosses παῖς as a household servant, to show the 'my' marks ownership and care, not shared nature.
'44' is a printed page number in the copy-text; skipped.
The section ends mid-sentence; the next section continues 'true Son and the true Spirit'.
